stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption behind using EAC to compare machines?
options: Each machine will be replaced by an identical one when it wears out
Costs and the discount rate stay the same in future replacement cycles
Each machine will be used once and never replaced
The need for the service continues indefinitely
explanation: EAC works because each option is assumed to repeat forever, so annual costs are the fair comparison. If a machine is used only once, simply compare PVs over the same service period.

stem: Why does the PV of costs used in an EAC calculation subtract the PV of the CCA tax shield?
options: CCA reduces the firm's taxes, which lowers the true cost of owning the machine
CCA is a cash outflow that has to be reversed
CCA is already included in the operating cost
CCA raises the discount rate
explanation: For a cost project, cash outflows are positive costs. The shield saves tax, so it is subtracted. The same is true of the discounted salvage value.

stem: Rental van X has an equivalent annual cost of $7,240 and van Y has $7,905. What does this mean?
options: Van X costs $7,240 in total over its life
Van X is cheaper by $665 for each year of service, so it should be bought
The two are equal because EAC removes all cost differences
Van Y is cheaper because its life is shorter
explanation: EAC is a cost per year of service. The lower the EAC, the cheaper the machine to provide the same service. The EACs, not the total PVs, are compared.

stem: In PV of costs for an EAC with taxes, which pair of items reduces the cost?
options: The after-tax operating costs and the salvage value
The purchase price and the PV of the CCA tax shield
The CCA tax shield and the after-tax operating costs
The PV of the CCA tax shield and the PV of the salvage value
explanation: PV of costs = purchase price + PV of after-tax operating costs - PV of salvage - PV of the CCA tax shield. Both salvage and the shield bring cash or tax savings back.

stem: Computing EAC for two machines with unequal lives gives the same ranking as chaining each machine's cash flows over their lowest common multiple of years.
options: True
False
explanation: The EAC method implicitly assumes the replacement chain repeats forever, so it picks the same machine as a replacement chain over the lowest common multiple of the lives.

stem: A 3-year machine has an EAC of $30,088 and a 5-year machine has an EAC of $29,138. Both will be replaced forever. Which should the firm buy?
options: The 5-year machine: it has the lower annual cost
The 3-year machine: its life is shorter and its PV of costs is lower
Either one: EAC is only for ranking, not for choosing
Neither: a cost can never be preferred
explanation: The firm minimizes cost per year of service. The 5-year machine saves $950 a year. The shorter life is already accounted for in its higher annual figure.

stem: Saskatoon Seed is choosing between press C and press D, both replaced forever. Press C costs $64,000, has pre-tax operating costs of $9,000 a year, lasts 4 years and sells for $14,000 (pool open). CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, T = 35%, k = 10%. What is press C's equivalent annual cost?
explanation: PV of costs = 64,000 + 9,000 x 0.65 x 3.1699 - 14,000/1.1^4 - PV CCA (12,023.37) = 60,958.16. EAC = 60,958.16/3.1699 = $19,230.52. Dividing by N, using the other press's annuity factor, ignoring the shield or leaving the operating costs untaxed each produce a different number.

stem: Press D costs $98,000, has operating costs of $6,500 a year before tax, lasts 6 years and sells for $16,000 (pool open); press C (4 years) has an EAC of $19,230.52. Same CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, T = 35%, k = 10%. By how much per year is the cheaper press cheaper than the other?
explanation: EAC of D = 87,649.49/4.3553 = 20,124.97. Press C is cheaper by 20,124.97 - 19,230.52 = $894.45 a year. Differences of raw PVs ($26,691.33) mix different lives.

stem: Prairie Haulage needs a loader and is comparing two models, each replaced by an identical model when it wears out. Model A costs $85,000, has operating costs of $12,000 a year before tax, lasts 3 years and sells for $25,000. CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, pool open, T = 30%, k = 11%. What is model A's equivalent annual cost, as a positive number?
solution: PV of operating costs = 8,400 x 2.4437 = 20,527.20; PV of salvage = 18,279.78
keystrokes: PV of costs first (see steps), then N = 3, I/Y = 11, PV = -PV of costs, CPT PMT

errors.label: Divided the PV of costs by N
errors.explain: A level annual cost with the same PV must be found with the annuity factor.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: The CCA shield lowers the cost of owning the machine.

errors.label: Used the other model's 5-year annuity factor
errors.explain: The annuity factor uses this model's own life, N = 3.

explanation: EAC = PV of costs (price + after-tax operating costs - salvage - CCA shield) divided by the annuity factor for its own life.

stem: Prairie Haulage's other loader, model B, costs $120,000, has operating costs of $8,500 a year before tax, lasts 5 years and sells for $20,000. CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, pool open, T = 30%, k = 11%. Model A has an EAC of $30,087.82. How much less per year does the cheaper model cost than the other? Answer as a positive number.

steps.label: EAC of A minus EAC of B

solution: PV of operating costs = 5,950 x 3.6959 = 21,990.59; PV of salvage = 11,869.03; PV CCA = 22,430.86
Model B is cheaper by 30,087.82 - 29,137.91 = $949.91 a year. Raw PV of costs would wrongly favour A ($73,526.04 versus $107,690.70)
keystrokes: PV of costs for B, then N = 5, I/Y = 11, PV = -PV, CPT PMT; subtract from A's EAC

errors.label: Compared the raw PVs of costs
errors.explain: Raw PVs hide the fact that B serves two more years.

errors.label: Divided each PV by its life
errors.explain: EAC uses the annuity factor, not N.

errors.label: Used a 3-year annuity factor for B
errors.explain: B lasts 5 years.

explanation: The longer-lived model has the lower annual cost even though its total PV of costs is higher.

stem: Bow River Cleaners buys a dryer for $14,000. It costs $1,100 a year to run, lasts 4 years and sells for $2,000. There are no taxes and k = 9%. What is the equivalent annual cost, as a positive number?
keystrokes: N = 4, I/Y = 9, PMT = 1100, CPT PV; add 14000; subtract PV of 2000; then CPT PMT

errors.label: Divided by N
errors.explain: Use the annuity factor, not N.

errors.label: Did not discount the salvage
errors.explain: The $2,000 arrives in 4 years.

explanation: No taxes: PV of costs over the annuity factor, with salvage reducing the cost.

stem: Kootenay Foods compares a packaging system that costs $210,000, needs $15,000 of working capital (recovered at the end), has operating costs of $31,000 a year before tax, lasts 5 years and sells for $18,000. CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, pool open, T = 40%, k = 12%, replaced forever. What is its EAC, as a positive number?
solution: PV of operating costs = 18,600 x 3.6048 = 67,048.84; PV of salvage and NWC = 33,000/1.12^5 = 18,725.09
keystrokes: PV of costs (steps above), then N = 5, I/Y = 12, PV = -PV of costs, CPT PMT

errors.label: Did not recover the NWC
errors.explain: Working capital is released at the end.

errors.label: Dropped the salvage term in PV_CCA
errors.explain: The machine is sold, so the shield on the salvage is lost.

errors.label: Divided by N
errors.explain: Use the annuity factor.

explanation: NWC goes in at time 0 and comes back at the end; everything else follows the same pattern.

stem: Athabasca Pipe Works forecasts its project's cash flows in constant year-0 dollars, with no allowance for price increases. Which discount rate is consistent with those flows?
options: The nominal rate
The inflation rate
The real rate
The effective annual rate
explanation: Flows in constant purchasing power are real flows and must be discounted at a real rate. Nominal flows, which include the expected price increases, use the nominal rate. Both give the same PV.

stem: The relationship between the three rates is (1 + R_nominal) = (1 + R_inflation) x (1 + _____).
options: R_effective
R_nominal
R_real
R_after-tax
explanation: The Fisher relationship compounds inflation and the real return. It is not the same as R_nominal = R_inflation + R_real, which ignores the cross term R_inflation x R_real.

stem: The word 'nominal' has two unrelated meanings in finance. Which pair of contrasts correctly states them?
options: Nominal versus effective (compounding), and nominal versus real (inflation)
Nominal versus real (taxes), and nominal versus effective (inflation)
Nominal versus after-tax, and nominal versus pre-tax
Nominal versus risk-free, and nominal versus risky
explanation: A nominal APR can be contrasted with an effective annual rate (compounding frequency). A nominal return can also be contrasted with a real return (purchasing power). The two are unrelated.

stem: Which of the following combinations is NOT consistent?
options: Nominal cash flows discounted at the nominal rate
Real cash flows discounted at the real rate
Nominal cash flows converted to real by dividing by (1 + R_inf)^i, then discounted at the real rate
Real cash flows discounted at the nominal rate
explanation: A real flow has no inflation in it, so a discount rate that includes inflation over-discounts it and understates the PV. The three consistent pairings all give the same PV.

stem: Why is the real rate not simply the nominal rate minus the inflation rate?
options: Because inflation is paid out of the real rate
Because purchasing power is a ratio: (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) - 1 is slightly smaller than R_nom - R_inf
Because the real rate is always zero when the rate is nominal
Because taxes are paid on the nominal amount only
explanation: At 10% nominal and 3% inflation, $1,000 grows to $1,100 while goods rise to $1,030: purchasing power grows 1,100/1,030 = 6.7961%, not 7%. The subtraction approximation drifts further for larger rates.

stem: A firm computes a project's EAC with real cash flows at the real rate and gets a lower annual cost figure than with nominal cash flows at the nominal rate, although both PVs of costs are identical. Why?
options: One of the two calculations must contain a mistake
Real cash flows are taxed less
The nominal rate is risk free and the real rate is not
The real annuity factor is larger, so the same PV spreads into smaller annual amounts; real dollars are 'today's dollars' while nominal dollars are future dollars
explanation: PVs agree because both methods are consistent, but EACs are expressed in different dollars. A real EAC is in constant dollars; a nominal EAC is a level nominal payment. Because the real rate is lower, the real annuity factor is larger, so the real EAC is smaller.

stem: Maple Ridge Mills forecasts a project's cash flows in nominal dollars and has a 12% required return that already includes expected inflation. What should the analyst do?
options: Subtract inflation from the cash flows and discount at 12%
Discount the nominal cash flows at 12%
Discount the nominal cash flows at the real rate only
Add inflation to 12% before discounting
explanation: The 12% includes inflation, so it matches nominal cash flows. Adjusting it again would double count the inflation effect.

stem: A nominal cash flow received in year i is converted to a real cash flow by dividing it by (1 + R_inflation)^i.
options: True
False
explanation: Dividing by cumulative inflation expresses the future dollars in today's purchasing power: CF_real,i = CF_nominal,i/(1 + R_inf)^i.

stem: Discounting nominal cash flows at the nominal rate and real cash flows at the real rate gives the same present value.
options: True
False
explanation: Both methods remove inflation from the comparison consistently. The nominal rate contains the inflation premium that the nominal cash flows also contain, and the real versions contain none.

stem: Foothills Gas expects 2.4% annual inflation and its required nominal return is 9.5% per annum. What is the real required return?
options: 6.93% per annum
7.10% per annum
11.90% per annum
12.13% per annum
explanation: (1 + R_real) = (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) = 1.095/1.024 = 1.069336, so R_real = 6.9336% per annum. Subtracting 9.5% - 2.4% = 7.10% ignores the cross term; multiplying the factors gives a nominal rate, not a real one.

stem: Bow Valley Ltd. must pay $10,000 a year in today's dollars (prices rise with 3% inflation, so the nominal payments grow at 3%) for 4 years. The nominal discount rate is 9% per annum. What is the PV of the payments?
explanation: Nominal flows are 10,300; 10,609; 10,927.27; 11,255.09. Discounted at 9% the PV is $34,790.17. Equivalently, discount 10,000 a year at the real rate 5.8252%. Discounting the real $10,000 at 9% ($32,397.20) mixes real flows with a nominal rate.

stem: Nechako Timber's required return is 8.2% per annum nominal and inflation is 2.6% per annum. What is the real required return, in % per annum?

errors.label: Subtracted inflation from the nominal rate
errors.explain: Real = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) - 1, not nominal minus inflation.

errors.label: Multiplied instead of dividing
errors.explain: Multiplying the factors gives a nominal rate from a real and inflation, not the reverse.

explanation: Divide the nominal growth factor by the inflation factor.

stem: Kootenay Foods wants a real return of 4.5% per annum on a project while inflation is expected to be 3.2% per annum. What nominal discount rate should it use, in % per annum?

errors.label: Added the two rates
errors.explain: The cross term R_real x R_inf = 0.144% is missing.

errors.label: Divided instead of multiplying
errors.explain: Nominal = real compounded with inflation: multiply the factors.

explanation: Fisher relationship, solved for the nominal rate.

stem: A 4-year service contract costs the firm $10,000 a year in today's dollars; prices rise with 3% inflation, so the nominal payments rise 3% a year from $10,300. The nominal discount rate is 9% per annum. Find the present value of the payments using real cash flows and the real rate.

steps.label: Check: PV of nominal cash flows at 9%

keystrokes: Real rate 5.8252%: N = 4, I/Y = 5.8252, PMT = 10000, CPT PV

errors.label: Discounted the real flows at the nominal 9%
errors.explain: Real flows must be discounted at the real rate.

errors.label: Used 9% - 3% = 6% as the real rate
errors.explain: The real rate is 1.09/1.03 - 1 = 5.8252%, slightly lower than 6%.

explanation: Two consistent routes: real flows at the real rate, or nominal flows at the nominal rate.

stem: A supply contract pays $250,000 in nominal dollars at the end of next year, then rises with inflation of 2.5% per annum forever. The nominal discount rate is 9.5% per annum. Find its present value by converting to real cash flows and discounting at the real rate.

steps.label: Check: nominal growing perpetuity D1/(R - g)

solution: Year-1 nominal 250,000 = 250,000/1.025 = 243,902.44 in today's dollars; real flows stay constant

errors.label: Discounted the real perpetuity at the nominal rate
errors.explain: Real flows need the real rate.

errors.label: Used 9.5% - 2.5% = 7% as the real rate
errors.explain: The exact real rate is 6.8293%, not 7%.

explanation: A growing perpetuity in nominal terms is a constant perpetuity in real terms.

stem: A 3-year machine has a PV of costs of $9,250, found with nominal cash flows at a nominal rate of 12% per annum. Inflation is 2.5% per annum. What is its equivalent annual cost in real (today's) dollars, using the real discount rate?
solution: For comparison the nominal EAC is 9,250/2.4018 = $3,851.23

errors.label: Used the nominal annuity factor
errors.explain: That is the nominal EAC. A real EAC uses the real rate in the annuity factor.

explanation: The PV is the same either way, but dividing by the real annuity factor gives the cost in constant dollars.

stem: A machine will be sold for $50,000 in nominal dollars at the end of year 5. Inflation is 2.5% per annum. What is the sale price in today's dollars (real terms)?

errors.label: Multiplied by the inflation factor
errors.explain: Today's dollars are worth more per dollar: divide, don't multiply.

errors.label: Used simple inflation of 12.5%
errors.explain: Inflation compounds: use (1 + 0.025)^5.

explanation: Deflate a future nominal amount by the cumulative inflation.
